title: Accelerated enzyme engineering by machine-learning guided cell-free expression
one_line: The authors built a cell-free pipeline coupling DNA assembly, protein expression and activity screening with machine learning to engineer amide synthetase (McbA) variants for multiple pharmaceutical amide products in about a week per campaign.
key_claims: Cell-free DNA assembly, expression and activity assay removes cloning steps, taking DNA design to activity data in hours rather than weeks.
Augmented ridge regression models trained on single-mutation data plus evolutionary predictions successfully predicted beneficial higher-order mutants while running on a standard CPU.
Nine specialised McbA variants were engineered with 1.6- to 42-fold activity improvements over wild type.
The campaign generated 2,856 enzyme variants tested across 12,584 reactions, with six pharmaceutical products optimised in parallel.
Moclobemide synthesis reached 96% conversion (42-fold improvement), scaled to milligram quantities, with stereo- and regioselectivity and enzyme stability maintained.
limitations: Demonstrated on a single enzyme scaffold (McbA) and one reaction class (amide synthesis), not across other enzyme classes.
Screening throughput remains a bottleneck, especially for products needing complex analytical detection.
Simple linear (ridge regression) models may not capture complex or epistatic fitness landscapes.
Predictions used activity data only; kinetics and stability were not incorporated into the models.
Scale shown was milligram, not industrially relevant conditions.
open_questions: Does the single-mutation-to-higher-order ML strategy transfer to other enzyme classes and reaction types with different fitness landscapes?
Would richer models or added kinetic/stability data improve hit rates over augmented ridge regression?
Can higher-throughput or selection-based readouts remove the screening bottleneck for hard-to-detect products?
How do the engineered variants perform at industrial scale and under process conditions?
